summary: Iowa law operates alongside United States federal law, which applies in the state. Gender identity has been removed from Iowa's civil rights statutes. The state had prohibited discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, housing and public accommodations since 2007; in February 2025 the Legislature passed a veto-proof bill removing that category, and Governor Kim Reynolds signed it with effect from 1 July 2025. Iowa became the first state to withdraw anti-discrimination protection from a group that already held it. A 2026 law then barred localities from maintaining civil rights protections stronger or broader than the state's, after several cities passed their own ordinances, with the capital city's protections dating to 1991. A transgender visitor who is refused service, denied housing or dismissed from a job in Iowa has no state-law remedy on the ground of gender identity.
tangentialFactors:
The July 2026 analysis 'Safe states don't make safer people' overlays the state legal-risk grading on Trans Murder Monitoring data and finds that legal-risk grades predict how a state behaves, not how people behave toward trans people; measured rates do not line up with the map's ordering, and the source states that every count is an undercount. Iowa is not named in that analysis, so its position in the violence data is not established by it. The practical inference is that Iowa's legal-risk tier describes the state's law and enforcement posture rather than a quantified level of threat from private violence.

The school facilities restriction is unusual in reach because it binds everyone on school grounds, not only students. An adult trans visitor attending a school event or visiting a campus is covered by the birth-certificate rule for multiperson restrooms and changing areas, and the single-person alternative is written as a student accommodation conditional on guardian consent.
localsOnly:
Conversion therapy is banned for minors in one city only. Davenport's council prohibited the practice on minors by an 8-2 vote on 22 April 2020. A statewide ban passed the Iowa Senate 26-24 on 17 March 2015 and died in the House, and in 2016 the state Board of Medicine and Board of Psychology declined to prohibit it by rule. Providers elsewhere in Iowa may lawfully offer it to minors.

Instruction on sexual orientation and gender identity is barred in kindergarten through grade 6 under a law signed in May 2023.

Parentage rules for couples read as same-sex under birth-sex status are comparatively developed. Joint adoption by married couples has been legal since a 2008 Iowa Supreme Court ruling, and individuals and married couples may adopt regardless of sexual orientation. State courts ordered that married lesbian non-birthing mothers be listed on death certificates (Buntemeyer v. Iowa Department of Public Health, 12 December 2012) and on birth certificates (Gartner v. Newton, unanimously affirmed 3 May 2013), so that support obligations and legal rights attach at birth. Lesbian couples have access to IVF with the non-genetic, non-gestational mother recognised if married, and Iowa courts have generally been favourable to gestational and traditional surrogacy although the state has no defined surrogacy statute.
outOfScopeNotes:
The Movement Advancement Project's equality map lists Iowa among states with an enacted ban on transgender people's use of facilities according to gender identity, but does not place Iowa in the group of states that define sex by birth in statute, while Senate File 418 imposes an unchangeable binary definition of sex determined at birth. The classification discrepancy is unresolved in the sources reviewed.

No Iowa statute restricting adult use of public restrooms or changing facilities outside school grounds is documented in the sources reviewed; the enacted facility restriction identified for Iowa is the school rule in Senate File 482.

How the 2025 statutory definition of sex interacts with Iowa's marriage framework, in force since 2009, is not addressed in the sources reviewed.

Enforcement of the school facilities rule against adults other than students, including staff, parents and visitors, is not documented beyond the statute's wording; districts were reported to be scrambling to comply when it took effect in 2023.

No Iowa-specific transgender homicide or violence figures appear in the sources reviewed, and the Trans Murder Monitoring-based analysis states that all such counts are undercounts.
